title: Remembering George Smoot
comment: LaTeX with figures (124 pages)
summary: George Smoot (1945-2025) was a major figure in observational cosmology, particularly through his role in the precision measurement of the CMB dipole and the discovery of the primordial CMB temperature anisotropy as part of the COBE team. This collection of 33 essays from collaborators, colleagues, students, and friends offers varied insights into the work, career, and life of George Smoot.

AI.tldr: This collection of 33 essays honors George Smoot (1945-2025), a key figure in observational cosmology known for precise CMB dipole measurements and the COBE team's discovery of primordial CMB temperature anisotropy.
AI.motivation: To provide varied insights into the work, career, and life of George Smoot through contributions from collaborators, colleagues, students, and friends.
AI.method: A curated collection of 33 essays written by people who worked with or knew George Smoot.
AI.result: A multi-perspective retrospective on Smoot's contributions to cosmology and his personal/professional impact.
AI.conclusion: George Smoot was a major figure in observational cosmology, remembered for his precision CMB measurements and discovery of primordial CMB anisotropy.

title: Here, There and Everywhere: How AGN jets affect galaxy cluster environments
comment: 17 pages, 11 figures, to be submitted to A&A. Comments welcome
summary: Active galactic nuclei (AGN) feedback via black hole-driven jets and winds plays a key role in redistributing matter across megaparsec scales. However, the implementation of jet feedback in cosmological simulations remains highly prescriptive, leading to uncertainties in the predicted state of the Warm-Hot Intergalactic Medium and other extragalactic observables. We investigate how variations in AGN jet velocity, orientation, and delayed hydrodynamic coupling impact the thermodynamic state of gas surrounding galaxy clusters. We aim to identify observational signatures in the thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ) effect and galaxy properties that can constrain these models. We employ zoom-in hydrodynamic simulations centered on three galaxy clusters from The Three Hundred, utilizing the SIMBA-C model and various feedback parameters. We use filament-finding algorithms and oriented stacking to probe the effect on large-scale structure and compare our results to observational data for brightest cluster galaxies from eRASS1, black hole-halo mass relations and baryonic mass fractions. Jet velocity is the dominant tested parameter in heating low-density environments at $z > 1$. At lower-$z$, higher velocity jets quench star formation, expel baryonic matter, and prevent black hole growth. While the tSZ signal within the central cluster and surrounding filaments is only affected by $\sim10\%$, the signal in under-dense regions outside filaments is enhanced by $\sim100\%$. In this case study, high velocity AGN jets provide the best match to galaxy properties from eRASS1 and other X-ray surveys. We find that hot gas in low-density regimes is a sensitive probe of AGN feedback. Future high-resolution tSZ surveys like the Simons Observatory and spectral-distortion experiments like FOSSIL have the potential to probe the thermal state of the gas outside clusters to distinguish between these feedback models.

AI.tldr: This study uses zoom-in hydrodynamic simulations of three galaxy clusters to investigate how variations in AGN jet velocity, orientation, and coupling impact the thermodynamic state of surrounding gas. Jet velocity is the dominant parameter: high-velocity jets quench star formation, expel baryons, and suppress black hole growth at low redshift. The tSZ signal is enhanced ~100% in under-dense regions outside filaments, and high-velocity jets best match observed galaxy properties from eRASS1 and X-ray surveys.
AI.motivation: AGN jet feedback in cosmological simulations remains highly prescriptive, causing uncertainties in predictions for the Warm-Hot Intergalactic Medium and extragalactic observables. The authors aim to identify observational signatures—particularly in the tSZ effect and galaxy properties—that can constrain these feedback models.
AI.method: Zoom-in hydrodynamic simulations centered on three galaxy clusters from The Three Hundred, using the SIMBA-C model with varied AGN jet velocity, orientation, and delayed hydrodynamic coupling. Filament-finding algorithms and oriented stacking are applied to probe large-scale structure, and results are compared to observational data (eRASS1 BCGs, BH-halo mass relations, baryonic mass fractions).
AI.result: Jet velocity is the dominant parameter. At z>1 it heats low-density environments; at lower z, higher velocity jets quench star formation, expel baryonic matter, and prevent black hole growth. tSZ signal changes ~10% in central cluster and filaments but is enhanced ~100% in under-dense regions. High-velocity jets best match eRASS1 and X-ray survey data.
AI.conclusion: Hot gas in low-density regimes is a sensitive probe of AGN feedback. Future high-resolution tSZ surveys (Simons Observatory) and spectral-distortion experiments (FOSSIL) can probe the thermal state of gas outside clusters to distinguish between feedback models.

title: The $H_0$ world cup. II. A comprehensive competition between proposed Hubble tension solutions
comment: 69 pages, 31figures, 16tables
summary: Cosmology stands at a crossroads. The Hubble tension has reached a nominal significance above $7σ$, while analyses combining DESI BAO and Type Ia supernova data show emerging hints of departures from $Λ$CDM. Meanwhile, high-precision CMB measurements from ACT and SPT enable a timely and more stringent reassessment of proposed solutions to the tension. In this paper, we revisit the $H_0$ Olympics, a systematic contest comparing proposed alternatives to $Λ$CDM using common datasets, likelihoods, and statistical criteria. In this updated edition, the $H_0$ World Cup, we subject fourteen representative solutions to a common analysis of current CMB, BAO, and SN data. The contenders span four broad mechanisms: late-time modifications of the expansion history, modified recombination, additional pre-recombination radiation, and early non-radiative energy injection. Relative to the original analysis, the present competition includes models and mechanisms proposed in the intervening years and evaluates all contenders using both Bayesian and Frequentist tests of tension and model performance, letting the neutrino mass sum vary. We further test if late-time extensions through curvature or the Chevallier-Polarski-Linder (CPL) dark energy parametrization can aid the success of the models. Finally, we subject the leading contenders to dedicated robustness tests involving alternative CMB likelihoods and multipole cuts, supernova samples, large-scale-structure information, and big-bang nucleosynthesis constraints. This framework assesses both the ability of each mechanism to ease the Hubble tension and the robustness of our conclusions to datasets and analysis choices.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the "H₀ World Cup," an updated systematic comparison of 14 proposed solutions to the Hubble tension, evaluated against current CMB, BAO, and SN data using Bayesian and Frequentist methods, with robustness tests across multiple datasets and analysis choices.
AI.motivation: The Hubble tension has reached >7σ significance, and new data from DESI BAO, Type Ia supernovae, ACT, and SPT show hints of departures from ΛCDM, necessitating a systematic and updated reassessment of proposed solutions to the tension using common datasets and statistical criteria.
AI.method: Fourteen representative solutions spanning four mechanisms (late-time expansion modifications, modified recombination, pre-recombination radiation, early non-radiative energy injection) are evaluated using common CMB, BAO, and SN data, with Bayesian and Frequentist tension tests, varying neutrino mass sum, testing late-time extensions (curvature, CPL dark energy), and applying robustness tests with alternative CMB likelihoods, multipole cuts, supernova samples, LSS data, and BBN constraints.
AI.result: The paper provides a comparative assessment of how well each mechanism eases the Hubble tension and evaluates the robustness of conclusions to different datasets and analysis choices, leveraging the latest high-precision data from ACT, SPT, DESI, and supernova surveys.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables a systematic and rigorous evaluation of Hubble tension solutions, testing both their ability to resolve the tension and the stability of findings across diverse datasets and methodological choices.

title: Evaluating the flexibility of the MillenniumTNG galaxy formation model with multi-zoom re-simulations
comment: 22 pages, 15 figures. Comments are welcome!
summary: In this study we introduce a new simulation campaign designed to understand how parameters that control star-formation and AGN feedback processes in cosmological hydrodynamical simulations impact observables such as the galaxy stellar-mass function (GSMF) and the gas fractions in large dark matter halos. These simulations are zoom-ins to halos selected from the MillenniumTNG (MTNG) simulation, and are run employing a novel multi-zoom approach which simultaneously re-simulates several sub-regions of a given large volume at a higher resolution than the background, thus reducing computational cost and imbalances in parallelization. We measure the GSMF and gas-fractions in halos for each of the re-simulations, and train Gaussian-process emulators on these quantities. The resulting emulators predict the GSMF and gas-fractions in halos with $\sim0.1\,\mathrm{dex}$ and $\sim 10\%$ precision respectively. Using the emulators we can simultaneously fit recent measurements of both quantities, in particular the lower gas fractions now observed even for comparatively massive clusters. Interestingly, we find a combination of parameters of the MTNG galaxy formation model that provides a qualitatively good fit to both the measured GSMF and gas fractions. This combination of parameters differs from the fiducial one mainly by requiring that stellar-feedback is significantly less energetic, and that kinetic AGN feedback events are significantly more energetic and rare. This finding implies that the MTNG model can be consistent with scenarios of strong feedback that remove large amounts of gas from groups and clusters, albeit we caution that we have not extensively examined the effect of these new parameters on many quantities for which MTNG made successful predictions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a multi-zoom simulation campaign to study how star-formation and AGN feedback parameters affect galaxy stellar-mass functions (GSMF) and gas fractions in halos. Gaussian-process emulators trained on these simulations achieve ~0.1 dex and ~10% precision. Fitting recent observations reveals that a parameter combination with weaker stellar feedback but stronger, rarer kinetic AGN feedback provides a good fit, differing from the fiducial MTNG model.
AI.motivation: To understand how star-formation and AGN feedback parameters in cosmological hydrodynamical simulations impact key observables (GSMF and gas fractions in halos), and to determine if the MTNG galaxy formation model can simultaneously match recent measurements of both quantities.
AI.method: A multi-zoom approach re-simulates sub-regions of the MillenniumTNG volume at higher resolution, selecting halos from MTNG. Gaussian-process emulators are trained on simulation outputs (GSMF and gas fractions) to predict these quantities with quantified precision (~0.1 dex and ~10%).
AI.result: Emulators achieve high precision. A parameter combination with significantly less energetic stellar feedback and significantly more energetic but rarer kinetic AGN feedback yields a good simultaneous fit to observed GSMF and lower gas fractions in massive clusters, differing from the fiducial MTNG model.
AI.conclusion: The MTNG model can be consistent with strong feedback scenarios that remove large amounts of gas from groups and clusters, though further testing on other successful MTNG predictions is needed before adopting this new parameter set.

title: Radial velocity statistics of cosmic voids as a probe of interacting dark energy
comment: 14 pages, 2 main + 2 appendix figures
summary: Due to their vast sizes and extremely low densities, the dynamics of cosmic voids are largely decoupled from complex, small-scale baryonic physics and are highly sensitive to the background expansion of the Universe. This makes them clean and sensitive probes of dark energy's properties. Using N-body simulations, we show that the void radial velocity and velocity dispersion profiles are sensitive to the Type 3 interacting dark energy model parameters, the momentum coupling $β$ ($<0$) and the scalar field parameter $λ$. Within the $1σ$ range of the best-fit values of $β$ and $λ$ constrained by Planck CMB, DESI BAO, and DES-Y5 supernova data, we find up to $\sim 30\%$ deviations in the void radial-velocity and velocity-dispersion profile spans relative to the uncoupled scenario, which can be well-approximated by a 4-parameter quadratic regression model. This demonstrates that the void radial velocity statistics provide an independent and observationally accessible probe of the dark-sector interaction in the Type 3 model.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that cosmic void velocity profiles are sensitive to Type 3 interacting dark energy model parameters (β and λ), with up to ~30% deviations from the uncoupled scenario within 1σ constraints, demonstrating that void radial velocity statistics serve as an independent probe of dark-sector interactions.
AI.motivation: Cosmic voids are clean, sensitive probes of dark energy because their dynamics decouple from small-scale baryonic physics and respond strongly to the background expansion, making them ideal for testing dark energy models.
AI.method: Using N-body simulations, the authors examine void radial velocity and velocity dispersion profiles as functions of Type 3 interacting dark energy model parameters (momentum coupling β < 0 and scalar field parameter λ), and compare results to the uncoupled scenario within 1σ ranges from Planck CMB, DESI BAO, and DES-Y5 supernova data.
AI.result: Up to ~30% deviations in void radial-velocity and velocity-dispersion profile spans relative to the uncoupled scenario were found; these deviations can be well-approximated by a 4-parameter quadratic regression model.
AI.conclusion: Void radial velocity statistics provide an independent and observationally accessible probe of dark-sector interactions in the Type 3 interacting dark energy model.

title: Dynamics in Nuclear Stellar Clusters: The Impact of Collisions and Disrupted Binaries
comment: 16 pages, 5 figures. Accepted for publication in ApJL
summary: The nuclear stellar clusters surrounding supermassive black holes (SMBHs) host millions of stars and stellar remnants. We study how stellar collisions and binary disruptions, alongside two-body scattering and gravitational-wave (GW) emission, shape the stellar distribution and regulate the abundance of stars on tightly bound orbits. We show the following. (a) Stars in the inner region of the cluster follow a steady-state density profile scaling as $n(r)\propto r^{-5/4}$, set by the balance between collisional depletion and binary replenishment. This profile is largely independent of whether two-body scattering or GW emission drives the orbital evolution prior to the collisions. (b) For SMBHs with $M\lesssim2 \times 10^7 M_\odot$, roughly half of the stars injected by the Hills mechanism eventually collide. The rest are tidally disrupted while on orbits with periods of order months to years. (c) For more massive SMBHs, these short-orbital-period tidal disruption events are suppressed, and most injected stars are ultimately destroyed by collisions. (d) Stellar extreme-mass-ratio inspirals (sEMRIs) can form around SMBHs with $M\gtrsim2\times10^6 M_\odot$, but are typically terminated by collisions before circularizing. Our model highlights the dynamical challenge stellar collisions pose for the formation of sEMRIs and, consequently, for stellar models of quasiperiodic eruptions. Applied to the Galactic Center, the collision-regulated density profile is consistent with the observed stellar distribution slope. Based on this profile, we estimate the stellar mass within the orbit of S2, finding it consistent with the observational upper limit, account for the recently discovered star S301, predict that most stars near Sgr$~{\rm A}^*$ follow eccentric orbits, and determine their typical eccentricities.

AI.tldr: This paper models how stellar collisions, binary disruptions, two-body scattering, and gravitational-wave emission shape the nuclear stellar cluster around SMBHs. Key findings include a steady-state density profile n(r)∝r^{-5/4} set by collisional depletion and binary replenishment; that for low-mass SMBHs (M≲2×10^7 M⊙) about half of Hills-mechanism-injected stars collide while the rest are tidally disrupted on month-to-year orbits; for higher-mass SMBHs short-period TDEs are suppressed and most injected stars collide; sEMRIs can form around SMBHs with M≳2×10^6 M⊙ but are typically terminated by collisions before circularizing. Applied to the Galactic Center, the model matches observed stellar slopes, explains S301, and predicts predominantly eccentric orbits near Sgr A*.
AI.motivation: To understand how stellar collisions, binary disruptions, two-body scattering, and gravitational-wave emission jointly regulate the distribution and dynamics of stars in nuclear stellar clusters surrounding supermassive black holes.
AI.method: Analytical modeling of steady-state density profiles balancing collisional depletion and binary replenishment, combined with analysis of orbital evolution driven by two-body scattering and GW emission, applied to SMBHs across a range of masses.
AI.result: (a) Inner cluster density follows n(r)∝r^{-5/4}. (b) For M≲2×10^7 M⊙, ~half of Hills-injected stars collide; rest are tidally disrupted on month-to-year orbits. (c) For more massive SMBHs, short-period TDEs suppressed, most injected stars collide. (d) sEMRIs form for M≳2×10^6 M⊙ but are terminated by collisions before circularization. Applied to Galactic Center: consistent with observed slopes, explains S301, predicts eccentric orbits near Sgr A*.
AI.conclusion: Stellar collisions pose a significant dynamical challenge for sEMRI formation and consequently for stellar models of quasiperiodic eruptions. The collision-regulated density profile provides a robust framework consistent with Galactic Center observations.

title: Evaporating cosmologically coupled black holes
comment: 19 pages, 3 figures
summary: Cosmologically coupled black holes (CCBHs), whose masses evolve in response to the cosmological expansion, have recently attracted significant theoretical and observational interest. Existing studies have treated CCBHs as purely classical objects, neglecting the effect of Hawking radiation (HR), which competes with the cosmological coupling (CC) mechanism. We take a first step towards studying evaporating CCBHs, adopting a quasi-adiabatic approximation in which the HR rate is evaluated at the instantaneous CCBH mass, and modeling the CC mechanism through the phenomenological scaling of the mass with the scale factor, $M \propto a^k$. We show that, depending on the coupling strength $k$, even late-time CC activation can significantly delay Hawking evaporation, or lead to asymptotic CC-dominated mass growth, with important implications. We set limits on the abundance of primordial CCBHs from $γ$-ray observations, finding limits which are weaker than their uncoupled counterparts, as CCBHs are kept farther from the endpoint of evaporation for a longer time. Unlike standard primordial black holes, the CCBH formation and present-day masses no longer approximately coincide, even for formation masses $M_{\text{form}} \gtrsim 10^{15}\,{\text{g}}$. Therefore, the same population of primordial CCBHs may be subject to evaporation limits through its past emission history, as well as to other limits (such as microlensing) through its present-day mass.

AI.tldr: This paper studies evaporating cosmologically coupled black holes (CCBHs), showing that cosmological coupling can significantly delay Hawking radiation depending on coupling strength k, leading to weaker observational constraints from γ-ray limits compared to standard black holes, and causing a divergence between formation and present-day masses.
AI.motivation: Existing studies of cosmologically coupled black holes treat them as purely classical objects, neglecting Hawking radiation. Since Hawking radiation competes with the cosmological coupling mechanism, a unified treatment is needed to understand the interplay between these two effects.
AI.method: The authors adopt a quasi-adiabatic approximation where the Hawking radiation rate is evaluated at the instantaneous CCBH mass, and model cosmological coupling through a phenomenological scaling M ∝ a^k, where a is the scale factor and k is the coupling strength.
AI.result: Depending on coupling strength k, late-time CC activation can significantly delay Hawking evaporation or lead to asymptotic CC-dominated mass growth. Limits from γ-ray observations on primordial CCBHs are weaker than uncoupled counterparts because CCBHs stay farther from evaporation endpoint longer. Formation and present-day masses no longer coincide even for M_form ≳ 10^15 g.
AI.conclusion: CCBHs are subject to both evaporation limits (through past emission history) and other limits like microlensing (through present-day mass), unlike standard primordial black holes. The coupling mechanism fundamentally changes observational constraints and phenomenological predictions.

title: When X-ray Features Hurt: Label Noise and Luminosity Overlap in Machine Learning Classification of AGN and Star-forming Galaxies
comment: 5 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to RASTI
summary: In a previous paper, we found that adding an X-ray flux feature to a Random Forest Classifier of active galactic nuclei (AGN) and star-forming galaxies (SFGs) decreased classification accuracy from 97.51% to 89.26%, a counterintuitive result given the prevailing theory that X-rays are a reliable AGN diagnostic. This paper investigates the source of that discrepancy through both astrophysical and machine learning lenses. On the astrophysical side, we show that the X-ray luminosities of AGN and SFGs in the sample substantially overlap across the canonical $10^{42}$ erg/s threshold, reflecting the moderate luminosity characteristic of an optically-selected SDSS sample and the contribution of high-mass X-ray binaries (HMXBs) to SFG emission. On the machine learning side, we argue that the BPT-derived training labels constitute instance-dependent label noise: label uncertainty is concentrated near the BPT demarcation line, where X-ray data would be most useful as a discriminator. We show that misclassified objects in 5-fold cross-validation cluster primarily near the Kewley demarcation curve, with a median distance of 0.130 dex compared to 0.748 dex for correctly classified objects (with Kolmogorov-Smirnov test results of $D = 0.701,\; p = 3.93\times 10^{-9}$ showing a statistically significant difference), and the X-ray feature exhibits permutation importance consistent with active harm to model predictions. We conclude that the discrepancy is consistent with a machine learning artifact compounded by an astrophysical overlap, and that future classifiers operating on optically-selected samples should employ independent label sources or noise-robust training methods.

AI.tldr: Adding X-ray flux to a Random Forest Classifier of AGN vs. star-forming galaxies decreased accuracy from 97.51% to 89.26%. This counterintuitive result arises from two factors: (1) astrophysical overlap—X-ray luminosities of AGN and SFGs substantially cross the canonical 10^42 erg/s threshold due to moderate luminosities and HMXB contributions; (2) machine learning artifact—BPT-derived labels constitute instance-dependent noise concentrated near the demarcation line, where X-ray data would be most useful. Misclassified objects cluster near the Kewley curve (median distance 0.130 dex vs. 0.748 dex for correct ones; KS test D=0.701, p=3.93×10^-9), and X-ray features show permutation-importances consistent with active harm.
AI.motivation: To resolve a previously reported counterintuitive result where adding X-ray flux—a theoretically reliable AGN diagnostic—degraded classification performance, by investigating the source of the discrepancy from both astrophysical and machine learning perspectives.
AI.method: Astrophysical analysis of X-ray luminosity distributions across the 10^42 erg/s threshold; machine learning analysis using 5-fold cross-validation, distance-to-boundary metrics, Kolmogorov-Smirnov testing, and permutation importance to examine label noise and feature harm.
AI.result: Misclassified objects cluster near the Kewley demarcation curve (median distance 0.130 dex vs. 0.748 dex for correct objects; KS D=0.701, p=3.93×10^-9). X-ray features exhibit permutation importance consistent with active harm to model predictions.
AI.conclusion: The discrepancy is consistent with a machine learning artifact compounded by astrophysical overlap. Future classifiers on optically-selected samples should use independent label sources or noise-robust training methods.

title: Testing string theory with combined cosmological probes: a case study for dark matter gravitons
comment: 3 pages, 1 figure, published in Research Notes of the AAS
summary: The string theory Swampland programme has resulted in distinct scenarios for the particle nature of dark matter. In this research note, I use combined cosmological probes to constrain the Dark Dimension scenario, which predicts that dark matter consists of decaying massive gravitons characterised by a time-dependent kick velocity. I first provide updated constraints using a combination of CMB and BAO data. I then produce forecasts for a Stage-IV tomographic survey, and outline strategies for predicting the model's behaviour on nonlinear scales. The results demonstrate the potential of surveys like Euclid and LSST to confirm or rule out string theory models of the dark sector.

AI.tldr: This paper uses cosmological data (CMB, BAO, and forecasts for Stage-IV surveys) to constrain the Dark Dimension scenario from string theory, where dark matter consists of decaying massive gravitons with a time-dependent kick velocity. Results show potential for Euclid and LSST to test string theory dark sector models.
AI.motivation: To constrain the Dark Dimension scenario from string theory Swampland programme, which predicts decaying massive graviton dark matter with a time-dependent kick velocity, using combined cosmological probes.
AI.method: Updated constraints from CMB and BAO data combinations, plus forecasts for Stage-IV tomographic surveys (Euclid, LSST) and strategies for modeling nonlinear scales.
AI.result: Demonstrates the potential of Stage-IV surveys (Euclid and LSST) to confirm or rule out string theory models of the dark sector.
AI.conclusion: Combined cosmological probes can effectively constrain string theory-inspired dark matter scenarios, with upcoming surveys capable of testing the Dark Dimension prediction.

title: COSMOS2025: A Machine Learning Census of Massive Quiescent Galaxies at $2.5 < \text{z} < 5$
comment: 17 pages, 12 figures, 6 tables, Accepted for Publication in ApJ
summary: The existence of massive quiescent galaxies at high redshifts ($ \text{z} \gtrsim 2$) strongly constrains the rapid quenching mechanisms in galaxy evolution models. We present a machine learning framework to identify massive ($\log(\text{M}_*/\text{M}_\odot) > 9.5$) quiescent galaxies at $2.5 < \text{z} < 5$ in the COSMOS2025 catalog. We train a \texttt{CatBoostClassifier} on mock photometry from the Santa Cruz semi-analytic models (SAMs), incorporating key JWST NIRCam bands and realistic noise to transfer the SAM-derived quiescent label (based on specific star-formation rate) to the observational space. When validated against the SAM ground truth, our classifier achieves a significantly higher recall (completeness) of 78\% (compared to 53\% for spectral energy distribution (SED)-fitting), while maintaining a high purity of 82\%. Applied to the COSMOS2025 sample, and assuming the SAM definition of quiescence transfers to the real Universe, the model identifies 1111 quiescent candidates, a population 2.6 times larger than the 427 candidates identified via the catalog's simple SED-fitting configuration. Under the SAM definition of quiescence, this consistent pattern of high purity but poor completeness suggests that the SED-fitting methods, constrained by simplified parametric star-formation histories, may miss a significant fraction of the quiescent population, likely galaxies in crucial transitional evolutionary stages. The trained classifier and classified COSMOS2025 sample are publicly available.

AI.tldr: This paper uses a machine learning classifier (CatBoost) trained on mock photometry from semi-analytic models to identify massive quiescent galaxies at z=2.5-5 in COSMOS2025. The method finds 2.6× more candidates than traditional SED-fitting (1111 vs 427), achieving higher recall (78% vs 53%) with good purity (82%), suggesting SED-fitting misses many transitional quiescent galaxies.
AI.motivation: Massive quiescent galaxies at high redshifts (z≳2) strongly constrain rapid quenching mechanisms in galaxy evolution models, but traditional SED-fitting methods may systematically miss them.
AI.method: Train a CatBoostClassifier on mock photometry from Santa Cruz semi-analytic models with realistic JWST NIRCam noise, transferring SAM-derived quiescent labels (based on sSFR) to observational space; apply to COSMOS2025 catalog.
AI.result: Classifier achieves 78% recall (vs 53% for SED-fitting) with 82% purity; identifies 1111 quiescent candidates vs 427 from SED-fitting—a 2.6× increase.
AI.conclusion: SED-fitting methods, constrained by simplified parametric star-formation histories, likely miss a significant fraction of the quiescent population, especially galaxies in transitional evolutionary stages.

title: A Universal Relation Between Primordial Density-Potential Cross-correlation Coefficient and Spin Factor Distribution
comment: submitted to ApJ, 6 figures, 2 tables
summary: Recent studies have revealed that the key properties of visible galaxies like their optical sizes, stellar ages, star formation rates and morphologies are closely linked with the angular momenta of their host dark matter halos. According to the linear tidal torque theory, the halo angular momentum, as a conserved quantity, is directly proportional to the primordial spin factor, $τ$, defined as the degree of misalignment between the principal axes of the initial density and potential Hessian matrices, which were found by numerical experiments to follow a Gamma distribution, fully characterized by its mean and variance. In this study, we heuristically develop an analytic expression for the mean and variance of $τ$ in terms of the initial density-potential cross-correlation coefficient, $q$. Analyzing a dataset from the Multiverse simulations performed for both of the flat $Λ$CDM and $w$CDM cosmologies, we prove that this analytic expression is universally valid in describing how the mean and variance of $τ$ change with $q$, regardless of the smoothing scales for both of the cosmologies. Given the prior finding that the $τ$-distribution can be reconstructed from the observable galaxy size distribution, this universal analytic expression may allow us to determine $q$ from the same observable via the mean and variance of $τ$. We discuss a possibility of constraining the early universe physics from the reconstructed $q$ via our heuristic model, without suffering from cosmological degeneracies.

AI.tldr: The authors derive an analytic expression for the mean and variance of the primordial spin factor τ in terms of the density-potential cross-correlation coefficient q, validate it universally across ΛCDM and wCDM cosmologies using Multiverse simulations, and propose that this relation enables constraining early universe physics from observable galaxy size distributions without cosmological degeneracies.
AI.motivation: To derive an analytic expression linking the mean and variance of the primordial spin factor τ to the density-potential cross-correlation coefficient q, and to explore its potential for constraining early universe physics from observable galaxy properties.
AI.method: Heuristic derivation of analytic expressions for the mean and variance of τ in terms of q; validation using the Multiverse simulations across flat ΛCDM and wCDM cosmologies at multiple smoothing scales.
AI.result: The analytic expression universally and accurately describes how the mean and variance of τ vary with q, independent of smoothing scale and cosmology (ΛCDM and wCDM).
AI.conclusion: The universal relation between τ statistics and q, combined with the ability to reconstruct the τ-distribution from galaxy size data, offers a pathway to constrain early universe physics without cosmological degeneracies.

title: Probing the Orientation Distribution of Nearby Double White Dwarfs through Gravitational Waves with LISA
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures
summary: We present a framework to study the orientation distribution of nearby double white dwarf binaries with LISA, explicitly accounting for the fourfold degeneracy in the polarization angle. Exploiting the belt-like sky distribution of the nearby sample along the Galactic plane, we show that the low-multipole extraction can be recast as an effectively one-dimensional Fourier analysis along Galactic longitude, within a spherical-harmonic expansion based on the Wigner-\(D\) formalism. The symmetry with respect to the Galactic plane governs the sensitivity: modes even under reflection across the plane remain accessible, while odd modes are strongly suppressed. For a fiducial sample of about 500 binaries within \(\lesssim 4\) kpc, corresponding to roughly 5\% of the resolved Galactic population, the method yields an uncertainty of order 0.02 for the even coefficients with \(\ell \leq 3\), and is readily applicable to the forthcoming LISA catalog.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a framework for analyzing the orientation distribution of nearby double white dwarf binaries with LISA, accounting for polarization angle degeneracy. Using a spherical-harmonic expansion based on Wigner-D formalism, they recast low-multipole extraction as a 1D Fourier analysis along Galactic longitude. Even reflection modes are accessible while odd modes are suppressed. For ~500 binaries within 4 kpc, they achieve uncertainty of ~0.02 for even coefficients with ℓ ≤ 3.
AI.motivation: To study the orientation distribution of nearby double white dwarf binaries using LISA observations, while properly handling the fourfold degeneracy in polarization angle.
AI.method: The authors use a spherical-harmonic expansion based on the Wigner-D formalism, recasting low-multipole extraction as a one-dimensional Fourier analysis along Galactic longitude. They exploit the belt-like sky distribution of nearby binaries along the Galactic plane and analyze symmetry with respect to the Galactic plane.
AI.result: For a fiducial sample of about 500 binaries within ~4 kpc (~5% of the resolved Galactic population), the method yields an uncertainty of order 0.02 for even coefficients with ℓ ≤ 3. Even reflection modes remain accessible, while odd modes are strongly suppressed.
AI.conclusion: The method is readily applicable to the forthcoming LISA catalog for studying the orientation distribution of double white dwarf binaries.

title: Supermagnified Stars in Lensing Clusters and Small-Scale Structure in the Dark Matter
comment: HWO Proceedings Part II: Mission Framework, Technology, and Broader Contributions
summary: Supermagnified stars, discovered by HST and JWST in lensing clusters of galaxies, are luminous stars in source galaxies lying near lensing caustics that are magnified by large factors ($\sim 1000$), making them detectable at cosmological distances. Intracluster stars in the lens modify the large-scale caustic into a corrugated network of micro-caustics, causing frequent microlensing events of the supermagnified stars. The frequency and lightcurves of these micro-caustic crossings are extremely sensitive to any small-scale, low amplitude surface density fluctations in the lensing cluster, making them a unique probe to dark matter minihalos or any small-scale irregularities. Furthermore, the disks of supermagnified stars can be resolved (at cosmological distances!) from photometric monitoring of micro-caustic crossing events, exploiting the limb darkening effect. Examples are shown of model lightcurves to fit the Kelly et al. (2018) observations of the first supermagnified star discovered. The unique sensitivity and angular resolution of the Habitable Worlds Observatory enables photometry of microlensing events of supermagnified stars sensitive to small-scale structure different from intracluster stars, a probe to the nature of dark matter that is not accessible to other observations at present.

AI.tldr: This paper discusses how supermagnified stars discovered by HST and JWST in lensing galaxy clusters can be used to probe dark matter minihalos and small-scale structure through micro-caustic crossing events, and how the Habitable Worlds Observatory could enable unique dark matter studies through photometric monitoring.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that supermagnified stars, magnified ~1000x by gravitational lensing, can serve as unique probes of small-scale dark matter structure (minihalos and irregularities) that are inaccessible to other observations.
AI.method: Analysis of micro-caustic crossing events caused by intracluster stars modifying large-scale caustics into corrugated micro-caustic networks; photometric monitoring exploiting limb darkening to resolve stellar disks at cosmological distances; model lightcurve fitting to Kelly et al. (2018) observations.
AI.result: Micro-caustic crossing frequency and lightcurves are highly sensitive to small-scale, low-amplitude surface density fluctuations; stellar disks can be resolved via limb darkening effects; HWO photometry can detect microlensing events sensitive to dark matter substructure beyond intracluster stars.
AI.conclusion: Supermagnified stars provide a novel and uniquely sensitive probe to dark matter nature and small-scale structure, with future Habitable Worlds Observatory observations offering capabilities not accessible to current instruments.

title: The different methods to calculate cluster membership probabilities
comment: 14 pages; 3 figures; 8 tables; submitted to A&A
summary: Reliable membership determination is a fundamental step in the study of star clusters. With the advent of $Gaia$ astrometry, a wide range of statistical and machine-learning techniques has been developed to assign membership probabilities. However, the current situation of membership lists is very unsatisfactory. This review summarises the main methodologies, compares their strengths and limitations, and discusses future directions. The aim is to provide a comprehensive overview and to lead to a more efficient and reliable approach for the forthcoming $Gaia$ DR4. Basically, we know of spatial, classical kinematic, and photometric methods, as well as maximum likelihood and Bayesian statistical methods, and machine learning and clustering algorithms. These different methods come with many modifications and flavours. We assessed all the advantages and disadvantages of the known methods to determine cluster membership probabilities. Although nowadays most methods are based on poor statistical numerics, the more robust algorithms should still be taken into account. It is important to apply and compare several methods. The next step must be to define a list of standard star clusters to test and verify all known methods. The list must cover the complete grid of cluster parameters (age, distance, reddening, and metallicity) and total masses.

AI.tldr: This review evaluates various methods for determining stellar membership in star clusters using Gaia astrometry, including spatial, kinematic, photometric, statistical, Bayesian, and machine learning approaches. It finds current membership lists unsatisfactory and advocates for standard star cluster benchmarks to systematically test and compare methods ahead of Gaia DR4.
AI.motivation: Reliable membership determination is a fundamental step in studying star clusters, but current membership lists are very unsatisfactory. This motivates a comprehensive review to assess existing methodologies and improve approaches for future Gaia data releases.
AI.method: The authors conducted a comprehensive review and comparison of methodologies for star cluster membership determination, including spatial methods, classical kinematic methods, photometric methods, maximum likelihood and Bayesian statistical methods, and machine learning/clustering algorithms, assessing their advantages and disadvantages.
AI.result: Most current methods rely on poor statistical numerics, though more robust algorithms exist. No single method is sufficient; applying and comparing multiple methods is important. The field lacks a standardized testing framework for method validation.
AI.conclusion: The next step must be to define a list of standard star clusters covering a complete grid of cluster parameters (age, distance, reddening, metallicity, and total masses) to systematically test and verify all known methods, leading to more efficient and reliable membership determination for Gaia DR4.

title: Adaptive optics imaging of the nuclei of Seyfert 2 galaxies: An unexpectedly high incidence of nuclear stellar rings
summary: High-resolution imaging of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) on subkiloparsec scales is essential for investigating their fueling. Observations in the near-infrared (NIR) are especially valuable as they minimize the absorption by dust. However, the inferred nuclear morphology may depend on the method used to analyze the images. We assess whether ground-based adaptive-optics observations of the cores of Seyfert 2 galaxies in the Ks band provide advantages over HST observations at shorter wavelengths (V and H bands). We also investigate whether a dedicated 2D analysis is preferable to a 1D approach. A sample of 18 Seyfert 2 galaxies was observed with the adaptive optics (AO) system in the Ks band at the Large Binocular Telescope (LBT) and compared to archival HST V- or H-band images. The analysis included a 2D modeling procedure via GALFIT as well as an unsharp masking technique. Results from different filters are consistent, showing no clear advantage of the redder filter. Using both GALFIT and unsharp masking in tandem is preferable, as the two methods provide complementary strengths. We identified nuclear stellar rings in 8 of the 18 galaxies in our sample (44 +/- 12%). This fraction is significantly higher than reported in previous studies and about a factor of two higher than reported in the most complete atlas of nuclear rings. The radii, size distribution, and inferred masses of the detected nuclear rings are similar to those observed in non-active galaxies. Low-luminosity AGNs appear to have little impact on nuclear ring formation and evolution. The high incidence of nuclear stellar rings in our study is unexpected and warrants further investigation. This could be tested further using the large number of suitable archival HST images available. If confirmed, it would imply that nuclear stellar rings are considerably more common than previously recognized.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes high-resolution NIR adaptive-optics observations of 18 Seyfert 2 galaxies, finding that nuclear stellar rings are present in 44% of the sample—twice the previously reported rate—indicating these structures may be far more common in AGN host galaxies than earlier recognized.
AI.motivation: High-resolution subkiloparsec imaging of AGNs is essential for understanding their fueling mechanisms. NIR observations minimize dust absorption, but it is unclear whether the inferred nuclear morphology depends on the analysis method, filter choice, or observational platform (ground-based AO vs. HST).
AI.method: 18 Seyfert 2 galaxies were observed with the LBT AO system in Ks band. Archival HST V- or H-band images were used for comparison. Both 2D modeling (GALFIT) and unsharp masking techniques were applied to analyze nuclear morphology across filters and methods.
AI.result: No clear advantage of the redder Ks filter over shorter wavelengths was found. Combining GALFIT and unsharp masking yields complementary strengths. Nuclear stellar rings were detected in 8/18 galaxies (44±12%), ~2× higher than the most complete previous atlas. Ring properties (radii, size, mass) resemble those in non-active galaxies. Low-luminosity AGNs show little impact on ring formation/evolution.
AI.conclusion: Nuclear stellar rings may be considerably more common in Seyfert 2 galaxies than previously recognized. This unexpected high incidence warrants further investigation using archival HST images.

title: Investigating anomalous microwave emission near G107.2+5.20 in Ku-band with the Green Bank Telescope
comment: 17 pages, 11 figures, submitted to MNRAS on 6/26/26
summary: Anomalous microwave emission (AME) is 30 GHz-peaking continuum emission thought to arise from spinning dust grains. Observations suggest that the local environment shapes the AME spectral energy distribution (SED), so building a spatially resolved sample of AME regions is a key step towards understanding its emission mechanism. Using the Green Bank Telescope Ku-band receiver, we obtained a ~1 arcmin resolution map of radius 1.25 deg centered on G107.2+5.20. Our first objective was to constrain the low-frequency side of the AME SED with 13 GHz data. Using matched-resolution aperture photometry, we measure the SED from 408 MHz-3 THz and fit two emission models: one including spinning dust, the other optically thick free-free emission. We find that the spinning dust model is superior, with an amplitude of $14.1\pm1.1$ Jy and a peak frequency of $27\pm2$ GHz. Our second objective was to spatially locate excess 13 GHz emission consistent with spinning dust. We compare our Ku-band map to multi-wavelength gas and dust tracers at ~4 arcmin resolution. We observe two sources of 13 GHz excess at 3$σ$ significance consistent with spinning dust emission, though potential contributions from optically thick free-free emission remain ambiguous. ``Region A'' (G106.95+5.19) is spatially coincident with peak dust radiance. ``Region B'' (G107.08+4.90) is spatially coincident with peak PAH abundance. If regions A and B are indeed sources of spinning dust emission, they are a resolved example of how AME-dust correlation varies with environment.

AI.tldr: Using the Green Bank Telescope, this study maps the region G107.2+5.20 at ~1 arcmin resolution, constrains the AME SED, and identifies two spatially resolved 13 GHz excess regions (A and B) consistent with spinning dust emission, showing how AME-dust correlation varies with local environment.
AI.motivation: Understanding the emission mechanism of Anomalous Microwave Emission (AME) requires spatially resolved samples to examine how local environment shapes the AME spectral energy distribution.
AI.method: The authors used the Green Bank Telescope Ku-band receiver to obtain a ~1 arcmin resolution map of a 1.25 deg radius region centered on G107.2+5.20. They performed matched-resolution aperture photometry from 408 MHz to 3 THz and fitted two emission models (spinning dust vs. optically thick free-free). They also compared the Ku-band map to multi-wavelength gas and dust tracers at ~4 arcmin resolution to spatially locate excess 13 GHz emission.
AI.result: The spinning dust model fits the SED significantly better, with amplitude 14.1±1.1 Jy and peak frequency 27±2 GHz. Two sources of 13 GHz excess at 3σ significance were identified: Region A (G106.95+5.19) coincident with peak dust radiance, and Region B (G107.08+4.90) coincident with peak PAH abundance.
AI.conclusion: If confirmed, Regions A and B provide a resolved example of how AME-dust correlation varies with environment, highlighting the role of local conditions (e.g., PAH abundance, dust radiance) in shaping spinning dust emission.

title: On the current status of tidal tails of Galactic open clusters
comment: 12 pages; 6 figures; 4 tables; submitted to A&A
summary: Tidal tails of open clusters provide direct observational evidence of cluster mass loss and dynamical interaction with the Galactic tidal field. The advent of $Gaia$ astrometry has enabled systematic detection of extended stellar structures around nearby clusters, revealing that many systems exhibit complex and extended morphologies beyond their classical tidal radii. In this review, we summarise the current observational and theoretical status of tidal tails in open clusters, focusing on results obtained in the $Gaia$ era. We compare different detection methodologies, including density-based clustering, probabilistic models, and orbit-based selection techniques, and discuss how methodological choices influence the inferred morphology of tidal structures. While the Hyades remains the most robust example of well-defined tidal tails, other clusters show a wide range of extended features with varying degrees of coherence and symmetry. We argue that the diversity of reported results reflects both genuine astrophysical variation and systematic differences in analysis approaches. We outline prospects enabled by upcoming astrometric, spectroscopic, and photometric surveys, which will allow a more unified and physically consistent understanding of cluster dissolution in the Milky Way.

AI.tldr: This review summarizes the observational and theoretical status of tidal tails in open clusters in the Gaia era, comparing detection methodologies and noting that diversity in results reflects both astrophysical variation and systematic differences in analysis approaches.
AI.motivation: Tidal tails provide direct observational evidence of cluster mass loss and dynamical interaction with the Galactic tidal field; Gaia astrometry has enabled systematic detection of these extended structures.
AI.method: The review compares different detection methodologies for tidal tails, including density-based clustering, probabilistic models, and orbit-based selection techniques, and discusses how methodological choices influence inferred morphology.
AI.result: The Hyades remains the most robust example of well-defined tidal tails, while other clusters show a wide range of extended features with varying coherence and symmetry. The diversity of reported results reflects both genuine astrophysical variation and systematic differences in analysis approaches.
AI.conclusion: Upcoming astrometric, spectroscopic, and photometric surveys will enable a more unified and physically consistent understanding of cluster dissolution in the Milky Way.

title: RABBITS IV: Stellar feedback and SMBH merging time-scales in the sub-Milky Way mass regime
comment: Submitted to MNRAS. 25 pages, 14 figures
summary: Merging supermassive black holes (SMBHs) in low- and intermediate-mass galaxies are important sources for future millihertz gravitational-wave observatories such as LISA. Predicting the delay between galaxy coalescence and SMBH merger is therefore critical for modelling the observable SMBH merger population. Using the KETJU code, we perform 16 equal-mass galaxy merger simulations as part of the Resolving supermAssive Black hole Binaries In galacTic hydrodynamical Simulations (RABBITS) series to investigate SMBH binary evolution in galaxies with stellar masses below $M_{\star}\lesssim10^{10}\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$. We systematically vary the strength of stellar feedback by altering the supernova outflow velocity by a factor of $\sim4$, while still producing galaxies consistent with observed scaling relations. We find post-hardening SMBH merger time-scales spanning $\sim30$-$500\,{\rm Myr}$, with stronger stellar feedback producing systematically longer merger delays through its impact on the central stellar density of the merger remnants. Across our suite, merging time-scales vary by more than an order of magnitude, demonstrating that uncertainties in stellar feedback alone can translate into large uncertainties in SMBH merger delays. At the onset of hardening, the binary evolution remains consistent with stellar-dynamical hardening models based on the local stellar density and velocity dispersion near the binary sphere of influence. Using KETJU as a benchmark, we show that merging time-scales can be recovered with useful accuracy when these nuclear stellar properties are extrapolated from scales up to $\sim 100\,R_{\rm infl}$. These results provide a promising route for modelling SMBH mergers in cosmological simulations.

AI.tldr: The RABBITS simulation series investigates SMBH binary merger delays in low-mass galaxies ($M_\star \lesssim 10^{10} M_\odot$) using the KETJU code. Varying supernova feedback strength causes merger time-scales to span ~30-500 Myr—over an order of magnitude—with stronger feedback leading to longer delays due to reduced central stellar density. Binary evolution during hardening follows stellar-dynamical models, and merger time-scales can be accurately estimated from nuclear stellar properties extrapolated up to ~100 $R_{\rm infl}$, offering a path for cosmological simulations.
AI.motivation: Predicting the delay between galaxy coalescence and SMBH merger is critical for modeling observable SMBH merger populations for future millihertz gravitational-wave observatories like LISA.
AI.method: 16 equal-mass galaxy merger simulations using the KETJU code, systematically varying supernova outflow velocity (by ~4×) to alter stellar feedback strength.
AI.result: Post-hardening SMBH merger time-scales span ~30-500 Myr; stronger feedback yields systematically longer delays. Merging time-scales vary by >1 order of magnitude due solely to feedback uncertainties. Binary evolution remains consistent with stellar-dynamical hardening models.
AI.conclusion: Merger time-scales can be recovered with useful accuracy by extrapolating nuclear stellar properties from scales up to ~100 $R_{\rm infl}$, providing a promising route for modeling SMBH mergers in cosmological simulations.

title: Mapping Dust Attenuation at Kiloparsec Scales. IV. A Dust-model Interpretation of Attenuation Curves in Nearby Galaxies
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures, submitted for publication in ApJ
summary: In this fourth paper on kiloparsec-scale dust attenuation, we ask whether the empirical trends found in Papers I--III can be translated into effective dust properties. Using attenuation curves for 2487 high-continuum-S/N spaxels in 91 SwiM v4.2 galaxies, we construct a grid of uniform-screen dust models composed of astronomical silicate and graphite grains with MRN-like size distributions. We fit the normalized attenuation-curve shape to constrain model parameters and then use the attenuation amplitude to estimate the model-dependent dust mass surface density. The inferred dust masses, compositions, and small-grain fractions are therefore effective quantities defined within the adopted attenuation model. The fitted models reproduce the main attenuation-curve variations and provide a direct bridge to Papers I--III: within this model, the relative 2175Å bump sequence maps mainly onto the effective fraction of small graphitic/carbonaceous grains, while the NUV-slope sequence maps onto the effective small-silicate grain fraction and total silicate mass fraction. Non-SF regions have higher dust mass surface densities but lower dust-to-stellar mass ratios than SF regions, separating absolute dust content from dust content per unit stellar mass. Regions with larger specific H$α$ surface brightness have larger dust-to-stellar mass ratios but lower inferred small-grain fractions, especially lower small-silicate fractions. In non-SF regions this quantity is interpreted as ionized-gas emission per unit stellar mass rather than as a direct sSFR. These model-dependent trends support a picture in which local dust processing changes the relative abundance of small grains and thereby shapes the attenuation-curve variations found across the series.

AI.tldr: This paper uses a uniform-screen dust model with astronomical silicate and graphite grains to fit attenuation curves for 2487 spaxels in 91 galaxies, finding that the 2175Å bump maps to small graphitic grain fraction, NUV slope maps to small silicate fraction, and non-SF regions have higher dust mass surface densities but lower dust-to-stellar mass ratios, supporting local dust processing shaping attenuation-curve variations.
AI.motivation: To determine whether empirical trends in kiloparsec-scale dust attenuation from Papers I–III can be translated into effective dust properties using a physical dust model.
AI.method: Constructed a grid of uniform-screen dust models (astronomical silicate + graphite, MRN-like size distributions), fit normalized attenuation-curve shapes for 2487 high-S/N spaxels in 91 SwiM v4.2 galaxies, then used attenuation amplitude to estimate model-dependent dust mass surface density.
AI.result: The 2175Å bump sequence maps to effective fraction of small graphitic/carbonaceous grains; NUV-slope sequence maps to effective small-silicate grain fraction and total silicate mass fraction. Non-SF regions have higher dust mass surface densities but lower dust-to-stellar mass ratios. Regions with higher specific Hα surface brightness have higher dust-to-stellar mass ratios but lower inferred small-grain fractions.
AI.conclusion: The model-dependent trends support a picture where local dust processing changes the relative abundance of small grains, thereby shaping the attenuation-curve variations found across the series.

title: The dynamical environment of the high-mass star-forming region G28.288$-$0.364
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures, Accepted for publication in Astronomy and Astrophysics
summary: Massive stars form within deeply embedded dust cores, and the development of hypercompact and ultracompact H II regions characterizes their early evolution. Identifying and analyzing such regions is essential for understanding the physical processes that govern massive star formation and the transitions between early evolutionary stages. In this article, we investigate the physical and kinematic properties of the massive star-forming region G28.288$-$0.364 to constrain the evolutionary stages of embedded H II regions and the surrounding cores. We analyze multiwavelength observations, including uGMRT radio continuum data; archival continuum and radio recombination line data from the GLOSTAR-D survey; high-angular-resolution ALMA Band 3 radio recombination line and 1.36-mm dust continuum data from the ALMAGAL survey; and complementary molecular line tracers. We derive spectral indices, measure linewidths and velocities of the radio recombination line emission, identify compact dust cores using dendrogram analysis, and estimate their physical properties. The radio continuum emission exhibits a positive spectral index, consistent with partially optically thick free-free emission. High-resolution observations resolve the ionized gas into two distinct components with physical sizes of $\sim$ 0.06 pc, and their RRL linewidths ($\sim$ 37 and 32 km s$^{-1}$, respectively) indicate that one component is in a transitional stage between hypercompact and ultracompact H II regions, while the other is more evolved. The 1.36-mm dust continuum data reveal five dust cores with surface densities consistent with the theoretical threshold for massive star formation. In summary, these results highlight the complex and sequential nature of massive star formation in clustered environments and demonstrate the importance of high angular resolution observations for resolving the early evolution of massive stars.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes multiwavelength observations of the massive star-forming region G28.288-0.364, resolving two ionized gas components and five dust cores. One ionized component is transitioning between hypercompact and ultracompact H II stages, while the other is more evolved, highlighting sequential massive star formation in clustered environments.
AI.motivation: Massive stars form within deeply embedded dust cores, and understanding the early evolution of hypercompact and ultracompact H II regions is essential for constraining the physical processes that govern massive star formation and the transitions between evolutionary stages.
AI.method: Multiwavelength observations including uGMRT radio continuum, GLOSTAR-D survey data, high-resolution ALMA Band 3 RRL and 1.36-mm dust continuum from ALMAGAL, and molecular line tracers. Spectral indices, RRL linewidths/velocities were measured, and dust cores were identified via dendrogram analysis with physical property estimation.
AI.result: Radio continuum shows a positive spectral index (partially optically thick free-free). Two resolved ionized gas components (~0.06 pc) with RRL linewidths of ~37 and 32 km/s indicate one is in a transitional hypercompact-to-ultracompact stage, the other more evolved. Five dust cores have surface densities meeting the theoretical threshold for massive star formation.
AI.conclusion: The results highlight the complex, sequential nature of massive star formation in clustered environments and demonstrate the necessity of high-angular-resolution observations for resolving early massive star evolution.

title: Even central galaxies feel their environment: cosmic siphoning of cool gas accretion
comment: ApJ in review
summary: Identifying the key processes regulating cool gas accretion in galaxies is essential for understanding the baryon cycle within galactic ecosystems. Recent studies indicate that the most fundamental internal process is likely the competition between halos and central black holes. This is revealed through a universal relation between increasing black hole masses and decreasing cool gas fraction ($μ_{\rm HI} \equiv M_{\rm HI}/M_{\star} \propto M_{\rm BH}^{-0.6}$). Here we further explore the primary external effects on cool gas accretion in central galaxies. We find that galaxies deviating significantly from the $μ_{\rm HI}-M_{\rm BH}$ relation are overwhelmingly isolated central galaxies without substantial satellites. These isolated, gas-poor centrals exhibit systematically higher black-hole-to-stellar-mass ratios and more prominent bulges, suggesting a greater susceptibility to AGN feedback. At larger scales, they are preferentially located near massive neighboring halos. We interpret these as evidence of "cosmic siphoning'' -- a multi-scale, gravity-driven process in which cool gas is channeled into deeper potential wells. On inter-halo scales, it manifests as competitive accretion: massive dark matter halos intercept cold filamentary streams, starving neighboring low-mass halos and quenching their star formation. On sub-halo scales, an analogous siphoning operates within groups and clusters, where the central galaxy systematically drains gas from its satellites through tidal interactions and accretion of satellite circumgalactic medium. This multi-scale mechanism -- from inter-halo competition to central-satellite interplay -- naturally drives the observed differences in the cool gas fractions between isolated and group centrals, or among the isolated, between those with and without a massive neighboring halo, and embodies a cosmic "rich-get-richer" paradigm.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a universal anti-correlation between black hole mass and cool gas fraction in galaxies ($μ_{\rm HI} \propto M_{\rm BH}^{-0.6}$), and introduces "cosmic siphoning" — a multi-scale, gravity-driven process where cool gas flows into deeper potential wells via inter-halo competitive accretion and sub-halo central-satellite interactions — to explain deviations from this relation, particularly in isolated, gas-poor centrals with massive neighboring halos.
AI.motivation: To understand the key internal and external processes regulating cool gas accretion in galaxies, specifically by exploring deviations from the universal $μ_{\rm HI}-M_{\rm BH}$ relation to identify external environmental effects on gas accretion.
AI.method: Analysis of galaxies deviating from the $μ_{\rm HI}-M_{\rm BH}$ relation, focusing on isolated central galaxies without substantial satellites, comparing their black-hole-to-stellar-mass ratios, bulge prominence, and proximity to massive neighboring halos.
AI.result: Isolated, gas-poor centrals deviating from the relation have systematically higher $M_{\rm BH}/M_{\star}$ ratios, more prominent bulges (indicating stronger AGN feedback), and are preferentially located near massive neighboring halos — supporting the "cosmic siphoning" model of competitive accretion on both inter-halo and sub-halo scales.
AI.conclusion: Cool gas accretion in galaxies is regulated by a multi-scale "cosmic siphoning" process (inter-halo competitive accretion and sub-halo central-satellite gas draining) that embodies a cosmic "rich-get-richer" paradigm, explaining differences in cool gas fractions between isolated and group centrals and among isolated galaxies based on neighboring halo presence.

title: The complex stellar system M 22: confirming abundance variations with high precision differential measurements
comment: 18 pages, 10 figures, 7 tables. Published in MNRAS
summary: M 22 (NGC 6656) is a chemically complex globular cluster-like system reported to harbour heavy element abundance variations. However, the extent of these variations and the origin of this cluster is still debated. In this work, we investigate the chemical inhomogeneity of M 22 using differential line-by-line analysis of high-quality (R = 110,000, S/N = 300 per pixel at 514 nm) VLT/UVES spectra of six carefully chosen red giant branch stars. By achieving abundance uncertainties as low as ~0.01 dex (~2 per cent), this high-precision data validates the results of previous studies and reveals variations in Fe, Na, Si, Ca, Sc, Ti, Cr, Mn, Co, Ni, Zn, Y, Zr, La, Ce, Nd, Sm and Eu. Additionally, we can confirm that the cluster hosts two stellar populations with a spread of at least 0.24 dex in [Fe/H] and an average s-process abundance spread of 0.65 dex. In addition to global variations across the cluster, we also find non-negligible variations within each of the two populations, with the more metal-poor population hosting larger spreads in elements heavier than Fe than the metal-rich. We address previous works which do not identify anomalous abundances and relate our findings to our current dynamical understanding of the cluster. Given our results, we suggest that M 22 is either a nuclear star cluster, the product of two merged clusters, or an original building block of the Milky Way.

AI.tldr: Using high-precision VLT/UVES spectra of six red giant stars in M 22, this study confirms significant chemical inhomogeneities (Fe, Na, Si, Ca, Sc, Ti, Cr, Mn, Co, Ni, Zn, Y, Zr, La, Ce, Nd, Sm, Eu), identifies two stellar populations separated by ≥0.24 dex in [Fe/H] and 0.65 dex in s-process abundances, and finds intra-population variations. The authors propose M 22 is either a nuclear star cluster, a product of two merged clusters, or an original building block of the Milky Way.
AI.motivation: To resolve the debated extent of heavy element abundance variations in the chemically complex globular cluster-like system M 22 and clarify its origin.
AI.method: Differential line-by-line analysis of high-quality VLT/UVES spectra (R=110,000, S/N=300 at 514 nm) of six carefully selected red giant branch stars, achieving abundance uncertainties as low as ~0.01 dex (~2%).
AI.result: Validated previous findings of variations in Fe, Na, Si, Ca, Sc, Ti, Cr, Mn, Co, Ni, Zn, Y, Zr, La, Ce, Nd, Sm, and Eu. Confirmed two stellar populations with ≥0.24 dex spread in [Fe/H] and 0.65 dex spread in s-process abundances. Non-negligible intra-population variations found, with the metal-poor population showing larger spreads in heavy elements.
AI.conclusion: M 22 is likely a nuclear star cluster, the product of two merged clusters, or an original building block of the Milky Way.

title: The complex stellar system M 22: constraining the chemical enrichment from AGB stars using magnesium isotope ratios
comment: 16 pages, 13 figures, 5 tables. Published in MNRAS
summary: The complex star cluster M 22 (NGC 6656) provides a unique opportunity for studying slow neutron-capture (s-process) nucleosynthesis at low metallicity due to its two stellar groups with distinct iron-peak and neutron-capture element abundances. Previous studies attribute these abundance differences to pollution from 3-6 solar-mass asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars, which produce significant quantities of the neutron-rich Mg isotopes 25Mg and 26Mg. We report the first-ever measurements of Mg isotopic abundance ratios at [Fe/H] approximately -2 in a globular-cluster-like system using very high-resolution and high signal-to-noise spectra (R = 110000, S/N = 300 per pixel at 514 nm) from the VLT/UVES spectrograph for six stars, three in each s-process group. Despite the presence of star-to-star variations in 24Mg, 25Mg, and 26Mg, we find no correlation with heavy-element abundances, implying that the nucleosynthetic source of s-process enrichment must not influence Mg isotope ratios. Instead, a key result of this work is that we identify correlations between 26Mg/24Mg and some light elements. Using a custom suite of AGB nucleosynthesis yields tailored to the metallicity of M 22, we find that low-mass AGB stars of approximately 1-3 solar masses are capable of reproducing the observed s-process abundances of M 22 and that the absence of any difference in Mg isotope ratios between the two s-process groups precludes AGBs with masses above approximately 3 solar masses. This places tighter constraints on possible formation scenarios and suggests an age difference of at least approximately 280-480 Myr between the two populations that is independent of isochrone fitting.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first measurements of Mg isotopic ratios at [Fe/H]~-2 in the globular cluster M22, finding no correlation with s-process enrichment. Using tailored AGB nucleosynthesis yields, the authors constrain the polluting AGB stars to masses below ~3 M☉, implying an age difference of ~280-480 Myr between the two stellar populations.
AI.motivation: To constrain the nucleosynthetic source (AGB star masses) responsible for the distinct s-process enrichment between the two stellar populations in the low-metallicity globular cluster M22 by measuring Mg isotopic ratios for the first time in such a system.
AI.method: Very high-resolution (R=110,000) and high S/N (~300) VLT/UVES spectroscopy of six stars (three per s-process group) in M22, measuring Mg isotopic ratios (²⁴Mg, ²⁵Mg, ²⁶Mg). Custom AGB nucleosynthesis yields were computed at the metallicity of M22 to interpret observed abundances.
AI.result: No correlation found between Mg isotope ratios and heavy-element (s-process) abundances, despite star-to-star variations in all three Mg isotopes. Correlations were identified between ²⁶Mg/²⁴Mg and some light elements. Low-mass AGB stars (1-3 M☉) can reproduce observed s-process abundances, while the lack of Mg isotopic differences rules out AGBs above ~3 M☉.
AI.conclusion: The polluting AGB stars were likely low-mass (1-3 M☉), excluding the previously proposed 3-6 M☉ range. This constrains formation scenarios and suggests a minimum age difference of ~280-480 Myr between the two populations, independent of isochrone fitting.

title: Magnesium isotope ratios in Milky Way and dwarf galaxy stars
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Published in MNRAS
summary: Under the assumption of hierarchical galaxy formation, dwarf galaxies are the closest existing analogues to the high-redshift protogalaxies that merged to form the Milky Way. These low-mass systems serve as unique laboratories for studying nucleosynthetic channels, given that the chemical compositions of their stars play a pivotal role in constraining their chemical enrichment history. To date, stellar abundances in dwarf galaxies have focused almost exclusively on elemental abundance ratios. While important, elemental abundances omit critical information about the isotopic composition. Here, we compute the Mg isotopic ratios of six accreted dwarf galaxy stars (low-alpha) and seven Milky Way stars (high-alpha) using a set of high-resolution (65000 < R < 160000) and high signal-to-noise ratio (S/N > 250) optical spectra. We show, for the first time, that at a given [Fe/H], stars born in a dwarf galaxy differ in their Mg isotopic ratios from stars born in the Milky Way. However, when comparing isotopic ratios at a given [Mg/H] rather than [Fe/H], a powerful diagnostic emerges that suggests nucleosynthesis processes are consistent across different stellar environments. This universality of Mg isotopic abundances provides additional dimensionality for chemical evolution models and helps to constrain massive-star nucleosynthesis across cosmic time.

AI.tldr: Using high-resolution optical spectra, this study shows that Mg isotopic ratios differ between dwarf galaxy stars and Milky Way stars at a given [Fe/H], but become consistent across environments when compared at a given [Mg/H], revealing a universality that constrains massive-star nucleosynthesis.
AI.motivation: Dwarf galaxies are analogues to high-redshift protogalaxies that merged to form the Milky Way. Their stellar chemical compositions are key to constraining chemical enrichment history, but prior work focused almost exclusively on elemental abundances, omitting critical isotopic information.
AI.method: Mg isotopic ratios were computed from high-resolution (65,000 < R < 160,000) and high signal-to-noise (S/N > 250) optical spectra for six accreted dwarf galaxy stars (low-alpha) and seven Milky Way stars (high-alpha).
AI.result: At a given [Fe/H], Mg isotopic ratios differ between dwarf galaxy and Milky Way stars. However, at a given [Mg/H], isotopic ratios are consistent across environments, suggesting universal nucleosynthesis processes.
AI.conclusion: The universality of Mg isotopic abundances provides additional dimensionality for chemical evolution models and helps constrain massive-star nucleosynthesis across cosmic time.

title: Cold Stream Penetration of Virial Shocks: Fragmentation, Coagulation, and Disruption in the Hot Circumgalactic Medium
summary: Cold streams penetrating virial shocks of massive halos along cosmic web filaments are expected to fuel galaxy growth at high redshift, yet the physical processes governing their penetration remain uncertain. We investigate cylindrical cold streams penetrating a hot circumgalactic medium (CGM) using idealized three-dimensional simulations. We systematically vary the stream radius, Mach number, and initial pressure contrast between the stream and the CGM across three density contrasts, while controlling stream properties after pressure equilibrium is re-established. We identify three evolutionary regimes: coagulation, fragmentation, and disruption, plus a borderline regime in which the stream core marginally survives while detached fragments are disrupted. At modest pressure contrast, survival is governed primarily by the competition between velocity shear and radiative cooling. Increasing pressure contrast produces a transient response during pressure restoration, temporarily enhancing or suppressing the cold-gas mass and cold-hot interfacial area before evolution converges to a shear-dominated state. At larger pressure contrasts, the oblique shock steepens into a bow shock, and the final outcome is determined by the ratio of the post-shock cooling time to the virial crossing time. In all survival cases, post-equilibration evolution is well described by turbulent radiative entrainment at the stream-CGM interface: the cold-gas mass flux increases while the mean streamwise momentum flux remains approximately conserved. Applying these results to a galaxy evolution framework, we find that cold streams in high-\ifmσ density peaks at $z>2$ are expected to survive and may fragment into multiphase structures embedded in the hot CGM. At $z\lesssim0.5$, stronger bow shocks and longer post-shock cooling suppress cold-stream penetration.

AI.tldr: Using 3D simulations of cylindrical cold streams penetrating hot CGM, the study identifies four evolutionary regimes (coagulation, fragmentation, disruption, borderline) governed by the competition between shear, radiative cooling, and pressure contrast. Survival requires short post-shock cooling time, and cold streams at z>2 are expected to survive, while at z<0.5 they are suppressed by stronger bow shocks and longer cooling.
AI.motivation: Cold streams along cosmic web filaments are expected to fuel high-redshift galaxy growth, but the physical processes governing their penetration through virial shocks of massive halos remain uncertain.
AI.method: Idealized 3D simulations of cylindrical cold streams penetrating a hot CGM, systematically varying stream radius, Mach number, pressure contrast, and density contrast, while controlling properties after pressure equilibrium.
AI.result: Four regimes identified: coagulation, fragmentation, disruption, and a borderline regime. At modest pressure contrast, survival governed by shear vs. cooling competition. Larger pressure contrast produces transient effects and a bow shock; final outcome depends on post-shock cooling time vs. virial crossing time. Post-equilibration follows turbulent radiative entrainment with conserved streamwise momentum flux.
AI.conclusion: Cold streams at z>2 are expected to survive and may fragment into multiphase structures; at z<0.5, stronger bow shocks and longer post-shock cooling suppress penetration.
